job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a recent health awareness drive at a local community center, experts emphasized that invisible microbes, not just visible dirt, are the primary cause of illness. Many residents mistakenly believe that if hands look clean, they are free of pathogens, but germs are microscopic and thrive even on surfaces that appear spotless. Furthermore, the experts clarified that soap does not instantly kill all germs; instead, it works by lifting oils and pathogens off the skin so they can be rinsed away with water. To be effective, this process requires scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, as a quick five-second rinse is insufficient to remove stubborn microbes. Regarding water safety, the community learned that boiling water is the most reliable method to eliminate pathogens. Simply heating water until it starts to bubble is not enough; it must reach a rolling boil for several minutes to ensure all harmful organisms are destroyed. Finally, the health team addressed the misuse of medicines, stressing that antibiotics are designed specifically for bacterial infections and are completely ineffective against viral illnesses like the common cold or flu. Relying on antibiotics for viral symptoms only contributes to the global problem of drug resistance, making future infections harder to treat.

items.evidence: Many residents mistakenly believe that if hands look clean, they are free of pathogens, but germs are microscopic and thrive even on surfaces that appear spotless.
items.q: Sam's hands look spotless after play. Why could they still make him ill?
options: Germs are too small to see by eye
Germs live only on dirty, smelly things
Germs spread only by a sick person's touch
Germs come from cold weather or getting wet
items.explain: Germs are microscopic, so they can stay on hands that look spotless.

wrong.why: thinks germs live only on dirty or smelly things
thinks germs pass only by a sick person's touch
thinks cold or wet weather brings germs

items.evidence: Furthermore, the experts clarified that soap does not instantly kill all germs; instead, it works by lifting oils and pathogens off the skin so they can be rinsed away with water.
items.q: How does soap help remove germs from our hands?
options: It lifts germs off skin so water rinses them
It kills all the germs the moment it touches
It adds little, as plain water cleans equally well
It seals germs under a coating on the skin
items.explain: Soap lifts germs and oils off the skin so they can be rinsed away, not killed instantly.

wrong.why: thinks soap kills all germs immediately
thinks water alone is as good as soap
invents a coating action not in the passage

items.evidence: To be effective, this process requires scrubbing for at least twenty seconds, as a quick five-second rinse is insufficient to remove stubborn microbes.
items.q: Meena rubs soap on her hands for a very short time. What is the likely result?
options: Her hands still keep some stubborn microbes
Her hands are germ-free after a quick rub
Her hands are safe because they look clean
Her hands are cleaner than after long scrubbing
items.explain: A quick rinse is not enough; scrubbing for at least twenty seconds is needed to remove stubborn microbes.

wrong.why: thinks a quick soap rub is enough
thinks hands that look clean have no germs
reverses the effect of scrubbing time

items.evidence: Simply heating water until it starts to bubble is not enough; it must reach a rolling boil for several minutes to ensure all harmful organisms are destroyed.
items.q: A family heats water only until bubbles start, then stops. What is likely true of this water?
options: Some harmful organisms may still survive in it
Every pathogen dies as soon as bubbles appear
Bubbles remove only the germs that are visible
Boiling never works; only filtering makes water safe
items.explain: Water must reach a rolling boil for several minutes; merely starting to bubble does not destroy all pathogens.

wrong.why: thinks a few seconds of heating makes water safe
thinks bubbles only affect visible germs

items.evidence: Finally, the health team addressed the misuse of medicines, stressing that antibiotics are designed specifically for bacterial infections and are completely ineffective against viral illnesses like the common cold or flu.
items.q: Why is it wrong to give antibiotics for a common cold?
options: It cannot treat a virus and fuels resistance
It cures colds but spreads them to others
It helps only if the cold came from rain
It works only against flu, not against colds
items.explain: Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses like colds, and misuse adds to drug resistance.

wrong.why: invents a harmful side effect not in the passage
thinks colds come from getting wet
mixes up cold and flu, though both are viral
